title: Finding the Sweet Spot for Teacher Autonomy
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene asks how much autonomy a classroom teacher should have and declines to offer a simple answer. Too little leaves a teacher reading a script and not really teaching; too much lets personal crusades bleed into professional practice. Drawing on thirty-nine years in the classroom, he offers rough guidelines, chiefly that the personal must not interfere with the work and that students must truly believe a teacher's beliefs will not affect how they are treated, taught or graded. He distinguishes real-person teaching from indoctrination, notes that high school sophomores are hard to indoctrinate, and warns about the teacher who says he only wants students to think but secretly expects them to reach his conclusion. The piece closes with the image of autonomy as a string that makes music only when pulled in opposite directions.
points: Teachers need real autonomy to adapt to teachable moments, but unlimited autonomy, including writing a whole curriculum alone, creates trouble for the school.
The working test is whether the personal interferes with the work: a photo on a desk is fine, a daily family update that displaces the lesson is not.
Students must believe a teacher's personal beliefs play no part in how they are treated or evaluated, or they learn to mimic the teacher's views.
Restraint and reflection are required, for instance avoiding essay topics where the teacher's feelings are so strong that bias might leak.
There is no hard line between personal and professional beliefs, so anyone offering a simple answer should not be trusted.
quotes: On the one hand, a teacher with no autonomy, who simply reads from the book or the canned script is not an actual teacher at all. If you're not bringing something to the classroom as a professional, educated adult, then why are you there? Some autonomy is absolutely necessary for real teaching.

But anybody who thinks that any of this would indoctrinate high school sophomores has never met a high school sophomore. All she managed to indoctrinate into us was the knowledge of which buttons to push in order to get her riled up and off track.

The best teachers are real people, and they bring their real people stuff into the classroom. Not all of it, and not all the time, but students do not respond particularly well to robot teachers. And teachers' real people stuff includes their beliefs and their values. We're hired to teach students to the best of our professional ability, and it's impossible to draw a hard, clear line between personal and professional beliefs.

But what you can do is make sure that your students believe--really, truly believe--that your personal beliefs will have nothing to do with how you treat them, teach them, and evaluate them in your class.

I've known a non-zero number of teachers who have sincerely said, "I don't want to teach students what to think--I just want them to think." But unfortunately, the unspoken--often unacknowledged second part of this was "And I will know they have really thought about this if they reach what I believe is the correct conclusion.

Teacher autonomy is one more string on the educational instrument, and like any string, it only makes music when it's being pulled in opposite directions. Too little autonomy and teachers can't do the work. Too much autonomy and teachers get in their own way of doing the work.
